meta.blurb: When Temujin's father is poisoned, his clan walks away and leaves the family in poverty. In 1206 the boy is named Genghis Khan, and his riders go on to reach from China to Poland. Here is how, and at what cost.
meta.bible: Genghis Khan: born Temujin about 1162 (year uncertain), elected ruler of all the Mongols in 1206, died 1227 aged about 65; burial place unknown. Temujin: his birth name. Yesugei: Temujin's father, a clan leader, poisoned. Hoelun: Temujin's mother. Borte: Temujin's wife, rescued after being carried off. Jamukha: Temujin's boyhood companion and later rival. Toghrul: an older ruler, Temujin's early ally. Tatars, Merkits, Naimans: rival peoples defeated. Ogedei: Genghis Khan's third son, great khan 1229 to 1241. Toregene: Ogedei's widow, regent. Sorghaghtani Beki: widow of a prince, mother of Mongke, Khubilai and Hulegu. Mongke: great khan 1251 to 1259. Khubilai Khan: great khan from 1260, founded the Yuan dynasty in 1271. Ariq Boke: Khubilai's younger brother and rival. Hulegu: Mongke's brother, took Baghdad in 1258. Batu: grandson of Genghis Khan, led the western campaign of 1236 to 1242. Subutai and Jebe: Mongol generals. Marco Polo: Venetian traveller who left in 1271 and returned in 1295; some scholars doubt parts of his account. The steppe: the grassland of Central Asia. Mongols, Mongolia, Karakorum: the Mongol capital built about 1235. Onon River, Gobi. Kuriltai: the great assembly of 1206. Yassa: the law code, contents uncertain. Yam: relay post system. Paiza: metal passport tablet. Gers: round felt tents. Uyghur: neighbouring people whose script the Mongols borrowed. Secret History of the Mongols: Mongol account written after his death. Western Xia, Jin, Song, Yuan, Ming: Chinese states and dynasties. Khanbaliq: Khubilai's capital, modern Beijing. Beijing, China, Yamen. Khwarazm: empire of the shah in Persia and Central Asia; Otrar: border city where a Mongol caravan was killed in 1218; Bukhara, Samarkand, Tabriz, Maragha. Caspian Sea, Caucasus, Black Sea, Kalka River: a battle in 1223. Cuman: steppe people. Kyiv fell in December 1240. Russia, Poland, Hungary, Sajo River, Europe. Baghdad: fell 1258; Abbasid: the caliph's dynasty. Mamluks: Egyptian rulers; Ain Jalut: battle of 1260. Egypt, Persia, Israel, Middle East, Asia, Mediterranean, India. Golden Horde, Ilkhanate, Chagatai: the other khanates. Japan, Java, Kamikaze. Black Death: plague of the 1340s. Mughal: dynasty of India. Venice, Islam, Muslim, Christian, Buddhist, Daoist. Eternal Blue Sky: the Mongol sky god. Voice and tone: clear, vivid and fair; battles and deaths are stated plainly and without gore; where historians disagree, the text says so; figures are approximate.

A1A2: Mongolia is a huge land of grass, wind and open sky.
The people there kept sheep and horses and moved with the seasons.
Children there learned to ride a horse when they were very small.
In those days, many tribes lived there and often fought each other.
A boy called Temujin was born on the grass long ago.
His father died, and the family had to live on very little food.
Enemies caught Temujin once, but he got away.
Temujin married a girl named Borte, and they began a family.
With help from friends, Temujin rode out and brought Borte home.
Many brave men joined Temujin because he was fair and strong.
Later, Temujin and his old friend Jamukha became enemies.
Temujin won many battles and beat all of his enemies.
In 1206, the people gave Temujin a new name, Genghis Khan.
He put his men in groups of ten, then a hundred.
Mongol soldiers rode fast and could shoot arrows from a moving horse.
Each soldier had many horses, so they could ride far each day.
They sometimes pretended to run away, and then turned to fight.
Genghis Khan wanted to keep records, so men began to write.
Everyone in the land had to follow the same rules.
People could follow many religions in the Mongol lands.
Next, the Mongols rode south to attack a rich walled kingdom.
They learned to use big machines to break down walls.
In 1211, the army went to war with northern China.
In 1218, a city in the west killed some Mongol traders.
The Mongols attacked, and many cities in the west were destroyed.
Two generals rode west to see new lands.
Genghis Khan died in 1227, and nobody knows where he lies.
After him, his son Ogedei became the new great khan.
Ogedei built a new capital city called Karakorum on the grass.
In 1234, the Mongols finished their war against northern China.
Next, a big army rode west into Russia.
In 1241 the army reached Poland and Hungary.
Mongol women were strong and important in the royal family.
Later, Mongke became khan and counted all the people.
In 1258, the Mongols attacked the great city of Baghdad.
In 1260, an army from Egypt stopped the Mongols.
Khubilai Khan became ruler of China and built a new capital.
In 1279, all of China belonged to the Mongols.
The huge empire split into four parts, each with its own khan.
Riders carried letters quickly from one station to the next.
Travellers carried a special tablet that let them pass safely.
Trade grew, and silk, spices and silver crossed the whole continent.
A young man from Venice travelled to China and wrote about it.
Doctors and star watchers from different lands shared their ideas.
In China, the Mongols used paper money instead of coins.
Two attacks on Japan failed because of terrible storms.
In the 1340s, a terrible sickness spread from Asia to Europe.
The wars killed many people and ruined many towns.
In 1368, the Chinese forced the Mongols out of China.
Today, Mongolia honours Genghis Khan as its most famous leader.
B1B2: Far to the north of China lies the steppe, a sea of grass that stretches for thousands of kilometres. Few trees grow there, and the wind blows almost without stopping.
The people of the steppe were herders, not farmers. They lived in round felt tents called gers, and they packed them up to follow fresh grass.
Steppe children learned to ride very early, often before they could walk well. By the time they were grown, a horse felt like part of their own bodies.
There was no Mongol nation at that time, only many tribes and clans. They raided each other for horses and pasture, and an old quarrel could last for generations.
A boy named Temujin was born near the Onon River in about 1162, although historians are not sure of the exact year. His father, Yesugei, was a minor clan leader who had many enemies.

When Temujin was still a boy, his father was poisoned by enemies, according to the old stories. The clan abandoned the family, and his mother, Hoelun, fed her children on roots, berries and small fish.
A rival clan once captured Temujin and put a heavy wooden collar around his neck. During a feast he escaped in the dark and hid in a river until the search had passed.
As a young man, Temujin married Borte, a girl who had been promised to him years before. Soon afterwards, raiders attacked the camp at dawn and carried her away.
Temujin asked two powerful allies, Toghrul and Jamukha, for help, and they agreed to ride with him. Their attack on the enemy camp was a success, and Borte was brought safely home.
Soon more and more riders chose to follow Temujin, and some of them came from rival clans. He gave important posts to men who were loyal and skilled, even if their families were poor.
Temujin and Jamukha had once sworn to be brothers and to stay loyal to each other for life. In time, however, they disagreed about how to lead, and each of them gathered an army against the other.
Over the next years, Temujin defeated the Tatars, the Merkits and other great rivals, one after another. He often invited the defeated to join his people instead of treating them as enemies.
In 1206, leaders from all the tribes met at a great assembly called a kuriltai. They gave Temujin the title Genghis Khan, a name whose exact meaning scholars still debate.

Genghis Khan organised his army into groups of ten, one hundred, one thousand and ten thousand soldiers. Men from different tribes were mixed together, so that old clan loyalties would not divide them.

Mongol soldiers shot arrows while riding at full speed, and they could even turn around in the saddle to shoot backwards. Their bows were short but strong, made from wood, horn and animal tendon glued together.

Every soldier brought several spare horses and changed from one to another during long rides. Because the horses took turns to rest, a Mongol army could cover much more ground than its enemies expected.
Mongol commanders sent out scouts to learn about the enemy long before a battle began. They sometimes pretended to run away, hoping that the enemy would chase them into a trap.
The Mongols had no writing system, so Genghis Khan took one from the neighbouring Uyghur people. Scribes then began to record laws, letters and the numbers of people and animals.
Genghis Khan made laws that were said to apply to everyone, rich or poor. Later writers called this body of law the Yassa, but historians are not sure exactly what it said.
The Mongols honoured the sky and the spirits of the land, but they did not force their religion on others. They often excused priests and monks from paying any taxes at all.
From 1205 the Mongols attacked Western Xia, a kingdom that lay between the steppe and China. The riders knew little about walled cities, so these early wars taught them a great deal about sieges.
Mongol leaders were quick to adopt skills that they did not have themselves. Engineers from China and Persia built giant machines that could hurl stones over city walls.
In 1211 Genghis Khan led his army against the Jin dynasty, which ruled northern China. After years of fighting, the Mongols captured the Jin capital, near today's Beijing, in 1215.
To the west lay the large empire of Khwarazm, which covered Persia and much of Central Asia. In 1218 a governor at Otrar had a Mongol trading party killed, and Genghis Khan demanded justice.

From 1219 Mongol armies swept through Khwarazm and took great cities such as Bukhara and Samarkand. Many people were killed and many cities were badly damaged, though historians still argue about how many.
While the main army fought in Persia, the generals Jebe and Subutai rode west with a smaller force. They crossed the Caucasus mountains and beat a Russian army at the Kalka River in 1223.
Genghis Khan died in 1227 while fighting Western Xia once more. He was about sixty-five years old, and the place where he was buried has never been found.
In 1229 the Mongol princes met in assembly and chose Ogedei, a son of Genghis Khan, as great khan. He was known as a generous and cheerful man who enjoyed feasts and drinking.
In about 1235, Ogedei built a capital called Karakorum in the heart of Mongolia. Craftsmen, merchants and visitors from many lands came to live and work in this new town.
Ogedei made an alliance with the southern Song dynasty, and together they destroyed the Jin state in 1234. Northern China was now Mongol land, and the Song would soon become the next target.
In 1236 a huge army under Batu, a grandson of Genghis Khan, rode west into Russia. The old general Subutai planned the campaigns, and by 1240 the Mongols had taken Kyiv.
In 1241 Mongol armies beat Polish and Hungarian forces, and fear spread across Europe. Then Ogedei died, and many historians think the princes turned back to choose a new khan.
Mongol women had more freedom and power than women in many neighbouring lands. After Ogedei died, his widow Toregene governed the empire for several years until a new khan was chosen.
In 1251 Mongke, another grandson of Genghis Khan, became great khan after years of quarrels. He ordered a census of people and animals, so that taxes were fairer and the empire was better run.
Hulegu led an army to Baghdad, the capital of the Abbasid caliph and a famous centre of learning. After a siege of about two weeks, the city fell in 1258, and the caliph was put to death.
In 1260 a Mongol force met the Mamluk army of Egypt at Ain Jalut, in what is now Israel. The Mamluks won, and the Mongol advance toward Egypt was stopped.

Khubilai, another grandson of Genghis Khan, won a struggle for power and became great khan in 1260. In 1271 he named his Chinese government the Yuan dynasty and built a new capital where Beijing stands today.
Khubilai spent many years fighting the Song dynasty, whose cities stood behind wide rivers and strong walls. In 1279 the last Song fleet was defeated at sea, and all of China came under Mongol rule.
The empire was too large to rule from one place, so it slowly split into four parts. These were the Yuan in China, the Golden Horde in Russia, the Ilkhanate in Persia and the Chagatai khanate.
The Mongols built a network of relay stations, called the yam, along the main roads. At each station a messenger could change to a fresh horse, so news travelled very fast.
Officials gave important travellers a metal tablet called a paiza, which worked like a passport. With it, a traveller could ask for food, fresh horses and a safe place to sleep along the road.
Merchants carried silk, spices, silver and fine pottery across Asia in greater numbers than ever before. Cities along the routes, such as Samarkand and Tabriz, grew rich and busy.
In 1271 a young man named Marco Polo left Venice with his father and uncle for the court of Khubilai Khan. His book about Asia amazed Europe, although some scholars doubt parts of his story.
The Mongol rulers often brought scholars from many different countries to live and work together. Persian astronomers worked with Chinese colleagues, and doctors compared their medicines and methods.
Khubilai's government in China printed paper money and required people to use it. Visitors were amazed that paper could buy goods, but printing too much of it later made prices rise.
Not every Mongol plan succeeded, and the sea proved a harder enemy than any army. In 1274 and 1281, Khubilai sent large fleets against Japan, but storms and strong defences ruined both attempts.
In the 1340s a deadly disease, known as the Black Death, spread from Asia to Europe. Many scholars think it travelled along trade routes, though the exact path is still being studied.
The Mongol conquests brought terrible suffering to many of the places they reached. Some regions took generations to recover, and historians still cannot agree on how many people died.
In 1368 a great rebellion drove the Mongol rulers out of China, and the Ming dynasty began. The other khanates also weakened, and the last Mongol overlordship in Russia ended in 1480.

The Mughal emperors of India took their name from the word Mongol, and they were proud of that ancestry. Today Genghis Khan is a hero in Mongolia, though in other countries his memory is a painful one.
C1C2: Across the middle of Asia, from the borders of China almost to the edge of Europe, there runs a great belt of grassland that people call the steppe. Few trees interrupt it, the winters are fierce, and the summers are short and dry, so farming is hard in most places. Yet this harsh and open country was the cradle of the largest land empire the world has ever seen.

The herders of the steppe measured wealth in animals and marked their year by the search for good grass, moving camp several times as the seasons turned. Their round felt tents, which the Mongols called gers, could be taken down quickly and loaded onto carts. A people who carried their homes with them learned to value speed, courage and a good horse above almost everything else.

On the steppe, a child was put on a horse almost as soon as he could sit upright, and the animal soon became less a possession than an extension of the rider's own body. Horses carried people, pulled their loads and gave them mares' milk, which was fermented into a sour drink. Anyone who has watched a horse and rider move as one will understand why the Mongols later felt that the whole world was theirs to cross.

Before the year 1200, the people we now call Mongols were divided into dozens of rival tribes and clans, each with its own leaders, its own herds and its own long list of old grievances. Raiding for horses, pasture and captives was a normal part of life, and a feud begun by a grandfather might be finished by a grandson. Peace, when it came, rarely lasted longer than the next quarrel over a stolen mare.

Temujin, the boy who would become Genghis Khan, was born in about 1162 near the Onon River, although the exact year is disputed because nobody on the steppe kept written records of such things. His father, Yesugei, led a small clan and had earned both a reputation for courage and a long list of enemies. Much of what we know about his childhood comes from the Secret History of the Mongols, a book written down after his death, which mixes sober fact with legend.

Yesugei was poisoned by enemies, the old account says, and the clan that had followed him promptly deserted his widow and children, believing that no one so poor could be worth protecting. Hoelun, his wife, kept her sons alive through a hard winter by digging for roots, gathering wild fruit and fishing in the river. Hardship of that kind, the storytellers insisted, taught the young Temujin that loyalty was precious and that a leader who could not protect his people had no right to lead them.

According to the old story, a rival clan once took Temujin prisoner and locked a heavy wooden collar around his neck, which made it almost impossible to eat, sleep or run. During a feast he knocked down his guard, slipped away in the darkness and lay hidden in a stream while his searchers passed within a few paces. One stranger who found him chose to help rather than betray him, and the young man never forgot what a single act of kindness could mean.

As a young man Temujin married Borte, the girl who had been promised to him years earlier, and her family gave him a fine black sable coat as a wedding gift. Not long afterwards, raiders from an old enemy attacked the camp at dawn and carried Borte away. It was the first great crisis of his adult life, and it forced him to look for friends powerful enough to help him.

Temujin turned to Toghrul, an older ruler who had been a friend of his father, and to Jamukha, a boyhood companion, and both agreed to ride with him. Their combined force fell on the enemy camp, scattering its defenders and bringing Borte home safely. The rescue showed the young man that alliances, rather than lone courage, were the true currency of the steppe, and it made his name known far beyond his own small camp.

Word spread across the grassland that Temujin shared plunder fairly, rewarded loyalty and promoted men for their ability rather than for the family into which they had been born. Herdsmen, hunters and even former enemies began to ride to his camp and swear to follow him. In a world governed by noble blood, this simple idea was almost revolutionary, and it gave him a following that no rich chieftain could buy.

The friendship between Temujin and Jamukha, once sealed with a solemn oath of brotherhood, slowly cooled as the two men came to disagree about how a leader should treat his followers. Jamukha favoured the old nobility and its privileges, whereas Temujin favoured talent, and the quarrel hardened until each had gathered a great army against the other. Their rivalry, which lasted for years, would end only when one of them had been defeated.

One by one, over the course of about two decades, Temujin defeated the Tatars, the Merkits, the Naimans and finally Jamukha himself, until no rival remained on the grasslands. Instead of leaving the beaten tribes to nurse their grievances, he mixed their families into his own and broke up the old clan loyalties that had caused so many feuds. The patchwork of quarrelling peoples was being hammered, slowly and sometimes brutally, into a single nation.

In the spring of 1206, the chiefs of every tribe gathered beside the Onon River for a great assembly, which the Mongols called a kuriltai, and proclaimed Temujin their supreme ruler. He took the title Genghis Khan, the exact meaning of which scholars still debate, though most agree that it carried the sense of a strong and universal leader. The scattered herders of the steppe had become, for the first time, one people with one name, the Mongols.

The new ruler organised his warriors by a decimal system, in units of ten, a hundred, a thousand and ten thousand, each with a commander who answered to the one above. Because the units were deliberately made up of men from different tribes, an old clan loyalty could no longer pull a soldier away from the army and toward his relatives. It was a framework of astonishing simplicity, and it let a single order travel quickly from the ruler's tent to the last rider in the line.

A Mongol warrior learned to loose arrows at a full gallop, and the best of them were said to release in the moment when all four hooves were off the ground, so that the shot flew true. His short composite bow, built up from layers of wood, horn and sinew glued together, was strong enough to throw an arrow farther than many enemy bows could reach. Years of practice since childhood made such skill ordinary rather than remarkable among the Mongols.

Each Mongol rider led a string of spare horses, switching from one tired animal to the next so that none was ever pushed past its limit. On the march he could also live on very little, drinking mares' milk and, in an emergency, it was said, a little of the blood of his horses, without even stopping to cook. The result was an army that could move in a day as far as an enemy's army could manage in several, and that appeared in places where nobody thought it could be.

Before a battle, scouts rode far ahead to study the enemy's strength, and during it, signal flags and drums let commanders direct thousands of riders across a wide field. One favourite tactic was the feigned retreat, in which a part of the army seemed to break and flee, drawing the pursuers out of formation until the main force closed around them. Discipline was the secret, because a false retreat that turned into a real one would be a disaster.

Because the Mongols had no script of their own, Genghis Khan borrowed the alphabet of the neighbouring Uyghur people, and a captured scholar was set to teach it to his sons. Within a few years the new writing was being used for letters, laws and the records of a growing state. Writing gave the young nation a memory, and it let the ruler's orders cross great distances without being changed by the mouths that carried them.

Genghis Khan issued a body of rules, later known as the Yassa, which was said to forbid stealing animals, protect messengers and punish those who betrayed their leaders. The original text has been lost, however, and historians still argue about how much of what is attributed to it was really set down in his lifetime. Whatever its exact words, the rules gave the new nation a sense that law came from the ruler's authority rather than from the whim of local chiefs.

The Mongols themselves honoured the Eternal Blue Sky and the spirits of mountains and rivers, yet they rarely tried to force their beliefs on the peoples they ruled. Buddhist monks, Muslim scholars, Christian priests and Daoist teachers were often excused from taxes, and a ruler might invite them to debate in his tent. Such tolerance was practical, since it kept conquered towns calmer, but it was also unusual in an age when many rulers persecuted those of other faiths.

Beginning in 1205, the Mongol armies struck southward at the kingdom of Western Xia, whose cities stood behind high walls that no horseman could simply gallop over. The early campaigns went slowly and taught the Mongols hard lessons about sieges, but in 1209 the Xia ruler agreed to become a loyal vassal. Having learned how to take a city, the young empire was now ready to look toward the greater prize of China.

Where the Mongols lacked a skill, they simply recruited it, and engineers, physicians and clerks from conquered lands soon marched with the army. Chinese and Persian specialists built catapults and other siege machines that could hurl heavy stones against walls, and some of their devices used early gunpowder. An army that had begun as pure cavalry was therefore becoming something more flexible and far more dangerous.

In 1211 Genghis Khan led his army across the Gobi and into the lands of the Jin dynasty, whose emperor ruled northern China from great walled cities. After several years of hard fighting and cruel sieges, the Jin capital, close to today's Beijing, fell to the Mongols in 1215. The conquest brought them more wealth than they had ever seen, but it also left them with the problem of how to rule a land of millions of farmers.

Westward lay the empire of Khwarazm, ruled by a shah whose lands stretched from Central Asia deep into Persia, and Genghis Khan at first sought peaceful trade with it. In 1218, however, the governor of the border city of Otrar seized a Mongol caravan and had its merchants put to death, and the shah then rejected the Khan's demand for justice. Convinced that his honour and his trade routes had both been insulted, the Mongol ruler prepared for war.

Within about two years, the armies of Genghis Khan overran the Khwarazmian empire, capturing Bukhara and Samarkand and pursuing the fleeing shah until he died alone on an island in the Caspian Sea. Cities that resisted were often destroyed, and their people suffered terribly, though the medieval figures for the dead are almost certainly exaggerated and modern historians disagree widely about them. Whatever the exact numbers, the damage to the region's farms, canals and libraries took generations to repair.

While the main army was busy in Persia, the generals Jebe and Subutai led a smaller force on an extraordinary ride around the Caspian Sea, over the Caucasus mountains and into the lands north of the Black Sea. In 1223 they crushed a combined Russian and Cuman army at the Kalka River and then turned for home, having travelled thousands of kilometres. It was less a conquest than a reconnaissance, and Subutai would return to those lands many years later.

In 1227, during a campaign against Western Xia, Genghis Khan died, probably from the effects of a fall from his horse or an illness, though the sources disagree. His body was carried back to the steppe, and the exact place where he was buried has never been found, despite many expeditions and countless legends. Having begun life as an abandoned boy, he left behind an empire that stretched from the shores of the Pacific toward the Caspian Sea.

Two years after Genghis Khan's death, the princes met in assembly and elected his third son, Ogedei, as great khan, as the old man had wished. Ogedei was generous, sociable and fond of wine, and he lacked his father's driving discipline, but he surrounded himself with able advisers and carried the empire's expansion forward. His reign showed that the Mongol state could survive the loss of its founder, which was no small achievement.

Around 1235, Ogedei had a permanent capital built at Karakorum, in the heart of Mongolia, with a walled palace, storehouses and districts for foreign craftsmen. Chinese artisans, Persian merchants and European visitors all passed through its markets, and in time the town held temples, mosques and a church side by side. Even so, the Mongol nobles remained at heart a travelling people who preferred their tents to the palace.

In 1234, with the help of the Song dynasty of southern China, the Mongols finally brought the long war against the Jin to an end and absorbed the whole north. The alliance did not last, because the Song soon quarrelled with their powerful neighbour over the territory that had been won. It would take the Mongols another forty-five years to finish what this victory began.

In 1236 an army commanded by Batu, a grandson of Genghis Khan, and planned by the veteran general Subutai, rode across the frozen rivers into the Russian principalities. City after city fell, and in December 1240 the great trading town of Kyiv was captured after a short siege. The Russian lands would live under Mongol overlordship for more than two centuries, and the shock of the invasion left a deep mark on their memory.

In the spring of 1241 the Mongols won decisive battles in Poland and at the Sajo River in Hungary, and the courts of Europe trembled at the prospect of a further advance. The army withdrew the following year, and although the death of Ogedei in December 1241 is the traditional explanation, historians still debate whether it was the only reason. Whatever the cause, western Europe was spared, and its rulers never knew how close they had come.

Mongol noblewomen managed households, herds and sometimes whole territories, and they enjoyed a freedom that astonished visitors from other countries. When Ogedei died, his widow Toregene ruled as regent for several years, and Sorghaghtani Beki, the wise widow of another prince, quietly shaped the education of the sons who would one day rule China and Persia. Few other great empires of that age, whether in Europe or in Asia, allowed women such visible and lasting influence over its rulers.

After a decade of quarrels among the princes, Mongke, a grandson of Genghis Khan and the son of Sorghaghtani Beki, was elected great khan in 1251. He was a serious and hard-working ruler who ordered a census, made the taxes more regular and tried to stop officials from taking more than their share. His brothers Khubilai and Hulegu were sent to extend the empire in China and in Persia, and the army moved out once more.

In 1258 Hulegu besieged Baghdad, the seat of the Abbasid caliphs and for five centuries one of the intellectual capitals of the Islamic world. The city fell after about two weeks, much of it was plundered and burned, and the caliph was put to death, which ended the Abbasid caliphate in Baghdad. Accounts of the death toll vary enormously, but all agree that its libraries, mosques and canals suffered terrible damage.

News that the great khan Mongke had died in 1259 forced Hulegu to withdraw much of his army, and the force left behind met the Mamluks of Egypt at Ain Jalut in 1260. The Mamluks, who had skilled horsemen of their own and chose their battlefield carefully, won the day, and the Mongol advance into the Middle East ended there. The victory showed that the Mongols could be beaten when they were short of men and horses.

Khubilai Khan, the brother of Mongke, won a struggle against his younger brother Ariq Boke and was proclaimed great khan in 1260, though not everyone in the empire accepted him. In 1271 he gave his government in China the dynastic name Yuan, and he made his capital at Khanbaliq, on the site of modern Beijing, where he built palaces, temples and wide, straight avenues. He wished to rule as a Chinese emperor as well as a Mongol khan, a difficult balance that he handled with considerable skill.

The conquest of the Song in the south was slow and difficult, because it meant crossing great rivers, besieging walled cities and building a navy, and the Mongols needed Chinese and Korean shipbuilders to do so. The last Song forces were crushed in a sea battle at Yamen in 1279, and for the first time the whole of China came under the rule of a foreign people. Khubilai now governed the most populous land on earth, and his wealth was the envy of every other ruler.

From a distance of several thousand kilometres, no single khan could govern lands from the Pacific to Poland, and after the 1260s the empire slowly divided into four great khanates. Khubilai's descendants ruled China as the Yuan, Batu's heirs held Russia as the Golden Horde, Hulegu's family governed Persia as the Ilkhanate, and the house of Chagatai kept Central Asia. The khans sometimes fought one another, yet they remained cousins and, for many decades, the routes between them stayed open.

The Mongols kept their enormous territory together with a relay-post network known as the yam, in which stations stood at regular intervals along the main roads, stocked with fresh horses, food and shelter. A messenger carrying urgent news could ride from station to station almost without stopping, covering distances in days that would normally take weeks. The villagers who supplied the horses and food, however, often found the burden extremely heavy, and many of them struggled to bear it for years.

Because the Mongols punished bandits severely and guarded the main roads, historians speak of a Mongol Peace, a period in which a trader could travel across Asia more safely than at almost any time before or after. Travellers of high rank carried a metal tablet called a paiza, which served as a passport and an order for food, horses and guides at every station along the way. The peace was bought by conquest, however, and it lasted only as long as the khans were strong enough to keep it.

Along the roads that the Mongols protected, caravans carried Chinese silk and porcelain, Persian carpets, Indian spices and silver from many countries, and the merchants who handled these goods often grew very rich. Cities on the main routes, among them Samarkand, Tabriz and Khanbaliq, filled with markets, inns and foreign quarters. Some of the Mongol princes themselves invested in trading partnerships, which allowed them to profit from the very commerce they had made safe.

Around 1271, a seventeen-year-old Venetian named Marco Polo set out with his father and uncle on a journey that would take them overland to the court of Khubilai Khan. When he returned to Europe, after about twenty-four years away, his account of the wealth of Asia astonished readers, but scholars still debate how much of it he saw himself and how much he heard from others. Even so, his book opened European imaginations to a world they had barely known.

Mongol rulers valued skilled people wherever they found them, and they moved scholars, craftsmen and doctors across Asia as if they were pieces on a very large board. Persian astronomers built an observatory at Maragha under Hulegu and exchanged knowledge with Chinese astronomers, while the study of medicine and the making of maps benefited from the same meeting of traditions. Knowledge, like silk, travelled further than before, and some of it eventually reached Europe.

Under Khubilai, the Yuan government issued paper banknotes backed by the state, and it required merchants to accept them in place of metal coins, which were scarce. Foreign visitors found it astonishing that a stamped sheet of paper could buy silk or grain, though the system worked only as long as the notes were not printed in excess. When later officials issued too many, prices rose sharply, and confidence in the paper currency slowly collapsed.

The Mongols were masters of the grassland, but at sea their advantages disappeared, and Khubilai's two great invasions of Japan, in 1274 and 1281, ended in failure. Japanese defenders, a stone wall along the coast and violent storms combined to wreck many of the ships, and a later expedition to Java also ended without success. Japanese tradition would call the winds kamikaze, or divine winds, and take them as proof that heaven protected the islands.

In the 1340s a disease that later generations called the Black Death spread across Asia and the Mediterranean and killed an enormous share of the people in many places. Many scholars believe that the plague moved along the trade routes and sea lanes that the Mongol era had made busier, although its precise origins and path are still being studied. The same connections that carried silk and ideas had also carried a deadly guest.

It would be dishonest to describe the empire only as a bridge between peoples, because its conquests killed a very great number of people and destroyed cities, farms and irrigation works that had taken centuries to build. Medieval chroniclers gave huge figures, which modern historians distrust, yet even the cautious estimates are sombre, and parts of Persia and Central Asia needed generations to recover. The truth about the Mongols is therefore double, for they were both destroyers and connectors, and a fair history must keep both in mind.

After the death of Khubilai, quarrels over succession, floods, famines and growing hostility to foreign rulers weakened the Yuan, and in 1368 rebel armies drove the last Mongol emperor north from Khanbaliq and founded the Ming dynasty. The other khanates endured longer, with several rulers converting to Islam, but one by one they dissolved, and the Golden Horde's grip on Russia loosened until it ended in 1480. By then the greatest land empire in history had faded into a set of smaller kingdoms and a vivid memory.

The Mughal dynasty of India, whose name comes from the Persian word for Mongol, ruled for more than three centuries and counted Genghis Khan among its ancestors. In modern Mongolia he is honoured as the founder of the nation, with his portrait on banknotes, whereas in the lands that were attacked, the memory of his armies is far darker. The Mongol story endures precisely because it holds both truths, a world connected and a world wounded, and each generation must weigh them again.
